\section[ōtium, ōtiī]{ōtium, ōtiī — leisure}

\label{lesson:LA-C274-otium}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for a grandson, then the Latin for a granddaughter.

\subsection*{You'll want to know: ōtium, ōtiī}
\textbf{ōtium, ōtiī} — \textquotedblleft{}leisure\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{ōtium} has no sure origin; no proposal is generally accepted.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[negōtium, negōtiī]{negōtium, negōtiī — business}

\label{lesson:LA-C274-negotium}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for a granddaughter, then the Latin for leisure.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: negōtium, negōtiī}
\textbf{negōtium, negōtiī} — \textquotedblleft{}business\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{negōtium} is \emph{nec}, \textquotedblleft{}not\textquotedblright{}, with \emph{ōtium}, \textquotedblleft{}leisure\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short): no leisure, so business. Festus already took it apart this way.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[lucrum, lucrī]{lucrum, lucrī — profit}

\label{lesson:LA-C274-lucrum}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for leisure, then the Latin for business.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: lucrum, lucrī}
\textbf{lucrum, lucrī} — \textquotedblleft{}profit\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{lucrum} is inherited, usually traced to Proto-Indo-European \emph{*leh2w-}, \textquotedblleft{}to take as booty, to profit\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB 2.1), with an ending for a means; German \emph{Lohn}, \textquotedblleft{}wages\textquotedblright{}, is a cousin (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for leisure, then the Latin for business, then say \emph{lucrum, lucrī} again

\section[damnum, damnī]{damnum, damnī — loss, damage}

\label{lesson:LA-C274-damnum}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for business, then the Latin for profit.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: damnum, damnī}
\textbf{damnum, damnī} — \textquotedblleft{}loss, damage\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{damnum} is usually traced to Proto-Indo-European \emph{*dh2pnom}, \textquotedblleft{}an outlay, an expense\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB 2.1), the source also of Greek \emph{dapanē}, \textquotedblleft{}expense\textquotedblright{}; Lewis \& Short still preferred a link with \emph{dare}, \textquotedblleft{}to give\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[dēbitum, dēbitī]{dēbitum, dēbitī — a debt}

\label{lesson:LA-C274-debitum}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for profit, then the Latin for loss.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: dēbitum, dēbitī}
\textbf{dēbitum, dēbitī} — \textquotedblleft{}a debt\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{dēbitum} is the past participle of \emph{dēbeō}, \textquotedblleft{}to owe\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB 2.1), used as a noun: what is owed. English \emph{debt} comes from it through French.
\end{cousinweb}

One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}
